Following the capture of Nicolas Maduro by U.S. forces in January, the U.S.-backed interim Venezuelan government has made changes to the legal, regulatory, and commercial frameworks, which has started to attract a broad pool of investors in its oil industry. Eni, Repsol, and Halliburton, to name a few, are back with deals to develop and help drill oilfields. U.S. supermajor Chevron has pledged over $7 billion in investment over the next five years to more than double its production in Venezuela to about 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) by 2031. The new oil order in Venezuela also includes North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), the company led by Venezuela-born businessman Alejandro Betancourt and involved in “the biggest oil deal in world history”. As much as $100 billion in investment could be involved in new oil infrastructure after the interim Venezuelan authorities granted NABEP 100-year concessions for 17 oilfields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels, according to the White House . Yet, NABEP could face challenges in hiring workers, competing for rigs, and securing capital to develop the huge resources in Venezuela, Reuters reported last week. The company disputed Reuters’ article, saying that the publication, even after receiving a detailed response to questions, ran only the parts that suited its “biased narrative” to question whether NABEP could deliver on its goals. This weekend, NABEP said its in-country fleet in Venezuela would reach in November a total of 41 of the 60 rigs announced in October. Currently, NABEP has nine drilling rigs that bore new wells in Venezuela. Three are active in the Junín 10 block of the Orinoco Belt, three more will start there soon, and three are being refurbished or moved into position. Four more rigs are being shipped from Houston, Brazil, and Colombia, the company said. “We are paying for every one of these rigs with the oil we produce. It’s the same reinvestment strategy we used to successfully grow production tenfold in two years,” NABEP CEO Alejandro Betancourt said in a statement. body: Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Africa now has a bank built to finance the oil and gas projects Western banks and development lenders have dropped under their climate commitments. Afreximbank and the African Petroleum Producers’ Organization (APPO) formally established the Africa Energy Bank (AEB) at its inaugural general meeting in Abuja on October 31. That was more than four years after the two institutions began work on it and some 20 months behind schedule. Abuja beat bids from six countries, including Ghana, Algeria, South Africa and Benin, to host the bank. Its first president is Helmy Ghazi, formerly deputy CEO of HSBC Bank Egypt, and a board drawn from the public sector, private sector and policy institutions will lead it. The AEB’s mandate covers the entire energy value chain: exploration and production, transport, processing, refining and distribution, cross-border pipelines and regional refineries, and power generation and transmission. The bank’s $5 billion in authorized capital is a ceiling. About $500 million has been mobilized so far, including $222 million from Afreximbank and a Nigerian contribution reported at between $100 million and $200 million. The AEB aims to mobilize up to $10 billion in financing in its first operational phase and plans to fund at least three projects in 2027, starting with regional refineries and pipelines. Its founders want to cut Africa’s dependence on imported petroleum products, expand intra-African energy trade, and finance “a just energy transition” in which African governments set the pace. The continent needs an estimated $200 billion in energy investment, and roughly 600 million Africans still lack electricity. Related: How Iran Just Broke the U.S. Oil Shield In Saudi Arabia Yet Again Africa received about $35 billion a year in energy finance from G20 countries and multilateral development banks between 2012 and 2021, according to a Carnegie report . The continent’s energy sector still faces a massive financing shortfall that existing channels have struggled to fill. Private money is flowing into African energy, but it is going to clean power, not oil and gas. Climate tech startups raised about $1.2 billion in 2025, or 38% of all venture funding on the continent, according to Africa: The Big Deal. Development lenders and commercial banks provided much of the money for clean energy: more than two-thirds of 2025 energy funding came as loans and structured facilities. Kenya alone took 29% of Africa’s startup funding last year, much of it in climate deals. In September, Nigeria launched a $300 million Distributed Renewable Energy Fund for solar mini-grids and off-grid power, backed by its sovereign wealth fund, Africa50 and SEforALL. The World Bank’s Mission 300 program is pushing in the same direction, with infrastructure investors overall putting $47.3 billion into African projects since 2012, and 81% of it went to energy and telecoms, according to the African Private Capital Association (AVCA). Hardly surprisingly, China continues to dominate Africa’s energy and mining sectors, providing much-needed capital through a combination of state policy banks, commercial loans, resource-backed agreements and integrated contractor packages. Through the so-called Angola Model , Chinese institutions provide large-scale loans for energy and infrastructure projects in exchange for long-term access to commodities like oil, copper and critical minerals. The extracted resources are either sold directly to Chinese buyers or used as collateral and direct repayment for the loans. The Export-Import Bank of China (Eximbank) and the China Development Bank (CDB) have lent $182 billion across Africa since 2000, mostly into the energy sector. body: Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy Simon Watkins is a former senior FX trader and salesman, financial journalist, and best-selling author. He was Head of Forex Institutional Sales and Trading for… U.S. President Donald Trump’s core vision of the future of global oil and gas is to have as much of that supply as possible coming from his self-proclaimed ‘Americas’ region, which is directly in the U.S.’s sphere of influence. Venezuela is one of the key countries from which this increased production is designated to flow, which is why Washington is focusing so much of its efforts on encouraging heavy investment from American oil and gas giants into the country. It is in this context that very recent changes to Venezuela’s ‘Organic Hydrocarbons Law’ should be seen. But are they ultimately likely to achieve their objectives? The details of these multiple changes to the law were definitively laid out over the past couple of weeks during and after the ‘Venezuela Global Investment Forum 2026’, which was part of a massive push by state oil firm Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (PDVSA) to lock in 105 new oil contracts by the end of this year. This was the first time the new government -- following the U.S. removal of former president Nicolás Maduro in January -- had delineated the exact tiered fiscal rates on a major international stage to tempt in global capital, despite the broad framework being technically written in January and clarified with fiscal regulations in July. In broad terms, the message presented by Venezuela’s vice minister of commercial policy, Ricardo Gomez, during and after the investment forum has been that the majority state control model for the oil and gas sector established under former president Hugo Chávez, and continued by Maduro, is over and that company operators can now have exclusive control over assets in the sector. Related: How Iran Just Broke the U.S. Oil Shield In Saudi Arabia Yet Again A crucial addition here is that Venezuela’s amended Organic Hydrocarbons Law has created new investment opportunities across its oil and gas sector, offering international companies varied contract options for developing heavy-oil reserves, mature fields, offshore gas resources and refining infrastructure. The new legal framework allows international investors to choose between hydrocarbon productive participation contracts, restructured joint ventures with state-owned PDVSA, and direct contracts covering infrastructure and oilfield services. For example, perhaps the most direct investment route for foreign firms into the country’s oil and gas sector is offered by the ‘hydrocarbon productive participation contracts’ (CPPHs). In this structure, a company incorporated in Venezuela operates a designated area at its own cost and risk for 25 years and, with ministerial approval, it will also have the legal right to sell its own share of the produced oil and gas directly to international buyers, completely bypassing PDVSA’s trading desks. This is a huge change from the Chávez/Maduro model, under which only PDVSA or another state-controlled entity had the legal monopoly to market and sell the crude. Under that structure, private partners were forced to let PDVSA handle the sales and then wait to be paid their share of the revenues -- a system that frequently led to foreign firms being trapped by PDVSA’s cash-flow crises, defaults, and the impact of primary US sanctions. This new CPPH model has already been used by Italy’s Eni, which transferred its Junín-5 heavy-oil field (with 35 billion barrels of certified oil in place) to this contract type in September, moving from a minority joint venture position to become the asset’s exclusive operator. title: Chile copper outlook worsens as price forecast rises
summary: The projected surplus of refined metal leaves little room for further supply disruptions.
body: Chile’s copper commission has cut its production forecasts for the world’s largest producer and raised its 2027 price outlook by 17% as mines struggle to recover lost output. Cochilco raised its average copper price forecast for next year to $5.95 per lb. from $5.10 in releases issued Friday. It now expects Chilean output to fall 8.4% this year, compared with the 2.6% decline projected in August. “The [global] surpluses we project are small and can change with operational delays or higher-than-expected consumption,” Executive Vice-President Claudia Rodríguez said in a price announcement Friday. The projected surplus of refined metal leaves little room for further supply disruptions. Demand just 1% above next year’s forecast would erase the surplus and create a deficit of about 65,000 tonnes if supply stayed unchanged, according to calculations based on Cochilco’s figures. BMO Capital Markets analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel said the downgrade could leave Chile with its weakest annual copper production in more than two decades. Cochilco raised its average price forecast for this year to $6.18 per lb. from $5.95. It still expects prices to ease 3.7% next year as supply recovers, but that decline depends on mines meeting their production plans and metal reaching consumers. Chile is expected to produce 4.94 million tonnes of the red metal this year and 5.08 million tonnes next year, down from the agency’s August forecasts of 5.27 million and 5.55 million tonnes, respectively. The country produced 3.63 million tonnes in this year’s first nine months, down 8.5% from a year earlier. BHP’s (ASX, LSE, NYSE: BHP) Escondida and Spence operations, together with state-owned Codelco, accounted for 77% of the net national decline . Cochilco points to lower ore grades, maintenance and interruptions affecting both the amount of material processed and the copper recovered. Reaching even the reduced annual forecast requires monthly production of about 434,000 tonnes in the fourth quarter, 7.6% above the average through September. Cochilco forecasts global mine production will rebound 3.4% next year to 24.08 million tonnes after slipping 0.6% this year. Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo would supply about 37% of that increase, making their recovery central to Cochilco’s market outlook. Chile would still produce 5.7% less copper than in 2025. Cochilco forecasts a refined-copper surplus of 144,000 tonnes this year, equivalent to 0.5% of consumption, widening to 215,000 tonnes next year, or 0.8%. Higher refining output, supported partly by intermediate stocks and recycled material, can coexist with falling mine production, it pointed out. The location of available metal adds to the strain. In its separate weekly market report, also released Friday, Cochilco recorded 1.05 million tonnes across the three principal exchanges. The U.S. exchange COMEX held almost 70% of the total, while Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks fell 18% during the week to 44,612 tonnes. China’s Yangshan import premium reached $205 per tonne, while cash copper on the London Metals Exchange traded $210 per tonne above the three-month contract on Thursday. Those premiums reflect the higher cost of obtaining metal for immediate delivery. Cochilco cautioned that fewer arrivals, shipping delays and contractual supply restrictions helped draw down Chinese stocks. The decline therefore doesn’t establish a broad acceleration in consumption. Demand offers less reassurance. Inflation has been running hot for more than five years, and Americans are feeling both the effects and the fatigue. The annual inflation rate was 3.6% as of September, according to the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, the Fed's preferred gauge. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 3.1%. Officials like Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh acknowledge that this is an "elevated" level. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023 (then held them steady last Wednesday). Warsh has insisted policymakers remain committed to long-run price stability, defined as 2% inflation — and not a bit higher. "The first thing we did when we showed up, with my colleagues, is we doubled down on the 2% inflation target. We said, 'We own it, we're taking responsibility,'" he said at a news conference Wednesday. "If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the 2's, let us disabuse you of it." Normally, economists say, a small amount of inflation is ideal for an economy. But after the steep price increases households have been forced to absorb, many Americans are wondering whether there could be a period of deflation, when prices don't just stop rising but actually fall, erasing some of those past gains. In other words: Will ad-free Netflix ever cost under $15 a month again? Or will average home insurance premiums drop below $2,000 a year? We reached out to five economists to ask for their inflation predictions. "Average prices as measured by CPI are up about 30% since 2019," says Daco, chief economist at EY Parthenon. "Consumers shouldn’t expect prices to return to where they were before the inflation surge, as that would likely require a significant economic downturn and sustained deflation; inflation should cool over time, but that simply means prices rising more slowly, not falling." "Prices coming down on average would be deflation. I do not expect deflation, nor should we want deflation. What we want is disinflation, which is a lower rate of inflation," says Meade, a research professor of economics at Duke University. Investors have grown increasingly worried that big tech companies are spending too much on AI data centers without clear evidence of when the investments will pay off. Amazon's heavy spending has pushed its free cash flow sharply lower. Many analysts remain bullish. UBS raised its price target on Amazon to $352 from $348 after the report, citing the outlook for AWS. Amazon is investing heavily in AI chips, data centers, robotics and its Project Kuiper satellite internet service. The company has also made large investments in AI developer Anthropic. Jassy has argued that strong demand for AWS and new opportunities in AI justify the spending and will deliver strong long-term returns. Monday's gain came as the broader market rebounded at the open. body: Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year. In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March. The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending. "We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down." Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter. The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity. When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

body: Oil fell nearly 4% on Monday as talks between Iranian and Qatari officials on a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran raised hopes that Middle East supply disruptions could ease. Iranian negotiators left Doha talks on Sunday, but not due to difficulties in negotiations, an official briefed on the meeting told Reuters on Monday. "The new month brought with it renewed hopes of a breakthrough in the Iranian stalemate," said Tamas Varga of oil broker PVM. Brent crude futures LCOc1 fell $4.20, or 3.7%, to $109.23 a barrel by 0900 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude CLc1 traded at $100.14, down $3.98, or 3.8%. Brent ended October at its highest in six months amid concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate again after Tuesday's US midterm elections. "Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now," said Tim Waterer, chief ⁠market analyst at KCM Trade. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran was prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". The talks follow a recent increase in attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, although there are also signs of shipments rising from some major exporters. In October, Saudi Arabia increased crude exports versus September despite attacks by the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, two of three ship-tracking companies said. The outbreak of the Iran war at the end of February has depleted oil stocks. title: Swiss inflation surprises higher in October but core prices offer some relief
summary: Switzerland October CPI +1.5% vs +1.3% y/y expected Prior +1.0% Switzerland October core CPI +0.5% y/y Prior +0.5% Swiss headline annual inflation picks up at the start of the third quarter, rising to 1.5% from 1.0% previously. Much like elsewhere around the region, higher energy prices are the main culprit in continuing to feed through to consumer prices. As such, the inflation numbers may look to be heating up again at first glance. But in looking to core annual inflation, that remains unchanged at just 0.5%. That tells us that the broader inflation picture isn't quite as alarming as the headline reading might suggest. And for the SNB, that is the most crucial takeaway here. The central bank has been arguing for months that higher energy costs are largely responsible for the inflation pickup, with limited evidence of second-round effects spilling over to the wider economy. The latest figures we're seeing today doesn't really challenge that narrative as such. Naturally, headline inflation moving closer to the 2% mark does mean that policymakers won't be entirely comfortable if energy prices continue to stay elevated. That will especially be the case if there is more evidence of businesses eventually passing those higher costs on to consumers. But at least for now, the SNB still has room to sit comfortably on the sidelines and assess how persistent these inflation pressures might become. In other words, there's no reason to panic just yet. title: Gold demand outlook weakens as high prices weigh on consumers - سانا
body: Damascus, Nov. 3 (SANA) Gold demand faces mounting pressure from elevated prices and expectations of higher interest rates, despite continued purchases by central banks and inflows into gold-backed investment funds, according to the World Gold Council (WGC) and commodities analysts at ING. The WGC lowered its forecast for growth in global gold investment demand in 2026 to 200 metric tons from 400 tons previously, citing weaker purchases of bars and coins. Global investment demand fell 14% year-on-year to 479 metric tons in the third quarter, as bar and coin purchases declined 19% to 268 tons. Jewellery consumption dropped 17% to 313 tons, its weakest third-quarter level since the council began collecting data in 2000. In India, the world’s second-largest gold consumer after China, annual demand is expected to fall to around 650 metric tons in 2026, its lowest level since 2020, as elevated prices and weakness in rural incomes weigh on purchases. The WGC said a weak monsoon and rising living costs were also likely to constrain demand, despite expectations of a seasonal recovery during the final quarter. Despite weaker consumer demand, central bank purchases rose 42% year-on-year to 321 metric tons in the third quarter, the highest quarterly level since the fourth quarter of 2024. Net purchases reached 675 metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, prompting the WGC to raise its full-year forecast. The council now expects central bank purchases to at least match the 848 metric tons recorded in 2025. Meanwhile, physically backed gold exchange-traded funds recorded inflows of 211 metric tons during the quarter, reflecting continued investor interest despite higher bond yields and a stronger US dollar. Gold’s recent recovery from a one-year low remains fragile, with expectations of higher interest rates and a stronger dollar limiting prospects for a sustained rebound, according to commodities strategists at Dutch bank ING. Analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said gold gained 1.85% on Monday, supported by lower oil prices and bargain hunting following last week’s sharp sell-off. They said easing tensions between the United States and Iran had pushed oil prices lower, easing inflation concerns and providing temporary support for the precious metal. However, higher interest-rate expectations, a stronger dollar and broader market volatility could continue to weigh on gold, limiting its recovery. Higher interest rates tend to reduce the appeal of gold, which does not generate interest income, while continued central bank purchases and investment fund inflows remain important sources of support.

body: Pecoy Copper , a Canadian explorer listed on the TSX Venture Exchange and the US over-the-counter market, has agreed to raise $49.8 million (US$35.7 million) from Hudbay Minerals and a second investor whose identity was not disclosed, Mining.com reported . The proceeds will fund drilling and technical studies at its copper -gold project in southern Peru, and the company's shares climbed on the announcement, which came on Monday. Hudbay's commitment totals $30.1 million, while the unnamed backer pledged $19.7 million. Calculated on a partially diluted basis, each would own just under 10% of Pecoy once the transaction closes. The deal ties Pecoy to a producer running the Constancia copper mine in Peru and supplies money for drilling and studies aimed at better defining the deposit and determining how its metals might be recovered. Bryce Adams, a mining analyst at Desjardins Capital Markets, called the transaction positive, noting that it confirms the technical and geological merit of Pecoy and bolsters the balance sheet with less dilution than his firm had anticipated. Andrew Dusome, a mining analyst at National Bank Financial , said in a separate note that Hudbay's lengthy operating record in southern Peru made the investment a robust vote of confidence in the project's future prospects. Pecoy stock gained 5.5% to $1.92 in Toronto on Monday morning, putting the company's value at roughly $405 million. Over the past year, the shares have ranged from 85 cents to $2.29. The Vancouver-based firm intends to issue about 24.7 million shares at $2.02 apiece, which is 10% above its 10-day volume-weighted average price through Oct. 30 and 11% higher than Friday's $1.82 close. The transaction is expected to close around Thursday, contingent on regulatory clearances, including TSX Venture Exchange approval. Hudbay would gain rights to join future financings and to top up its stake to preserve ownership of as much as 9.9%. Depending on ownership thresholds, it could appoint one director, or two should Pecoy's board grow to at least 10 members. CEO Vincent Metcalfe told The Northern Miner by email that both Hudbay and the unnamed investor had previously put money into Pecoy. Hudbay assembled its position through market purchases, while the second investor holds historical warrants that remain unexercised, he said. According to Adams, the financing would raise Pecoy's cash resources to approximately $70 million, sufficient for five to six quarters of expenditure. His model had presumed a $50-million raise at $1.50 per share, which would have required about 33.3 million new shares. Eric Winmill, a mining analyst at Scotiabank , wrote that the financing also enhances funding visibility through the coming phase of resource definition and technical work. The explorer holds the Pecoy and Tororume projects in southern Peru's Arequipa region. Pecoy sits roughly 275 km northwest of Arequipa at an elevation of about 1,650 metres, close to highway, power and port infrastructure. An April 2025 resource estimate set out 865 million inferred tonnes grading 0.34% copper, 0.012% molybdenum, 0.05 gram gold per tonne and 1.33 grams silver , for contained metal of about 6.45 billion lb. copper. The estimate applies a 0.23% copper cut-off, and the resources have not shown economic viability. Tororume, 8 km to the north, offers an additional exploration target. Prior owner Pembrook drilled nine widely spaced holes between 2017 and 2023, hitting copper and molybdenum mineralization, and Pecoy says much of the system has yet to be tested. body: Brent crude oil could reach $140/bbl and average ~$130/bbl next year if Persian Gulf oil production remains significantly below pre-war levels, Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note Monday. In this upside scenario, production would come in ~3.5M bbl/day below its 2025 average, compared with 1.1M bbl/day above the 2025 norm in the bank's base case. "The most likely price-upside triggers are intensified shipping attacks, damage to oil infrastructure, and a more persistent risk premium," Goldman analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby wrote. On the other hand, the bank said Brent could fall into the $60s if Persian Gulf production recovers faster than expected, rising to 2.5M bbl/day above 2025 levels, if the U.S. and Iran reach a deal that markets perceive as sustainable. Goldman raised its price forecasts for year-end 2026 and full-year 2027, saying it now expects Brent to average $105/bbl in December 2026 and $88/bbl overall in 2027, up from previous forecasts of $90 and $80, respectively, as persistent Middle East supply risks are expected to sustain a sizable geopolitical risk premium in the near term. "We now expect markets to price in a higher risk premium, reflecting downside risks to Mideast supply, the length of past major oil supply shocks, and many market participants’ view that a lasting diplomatic breakthrough will be difficult," Goldman wrote. "With the timing and location of disruptions nearly impossible to predict, our base case now includes a 1M bbl/day global supply disruption allowance in 2027," the bank wrote. Goldman also said a geopolitical risk premium of ~$27/bbl accounted for most of October’s oil price rally, while Brent’s fair value remained broadly stable in the $90s, as global inventories were little changed. The tell in episodes of this kind is whether the sell-off extends through the session or stalls once the headline is absorbed; sustained downside has historically required concrete deliverables, a signed framework or verified de-escalation, rather than draft proposals and goodwill signalling. The offsetting fundamentals here are familiar counterweights: OPEC+ holding quotas steady and a major bank lifting its price view are the kind of supply-side anchors that have tended to put a floor under diplomacy-driven dips unless demand concerns dominate. TTF moving in sympathy is the standard European gas read-across, where the same risk premium unwinds faster given thinner liquidity. Gold and silver firming as energy softens, alongside a weaker dollar, fits the recurring pattern of the metals complex trading the currency and rate channel rather than the geopolitical one once the immediate fear premium fades. Worth noting is the calendar risk inherent in headline-driven sessions: 'follow-up meeting possible' leaves the tape exposed to the next round of mediator commentary, which in past sequences has been the trigger for partial retracement.

body: Australia’s biggest bank has issued a bleak warning about the state of the economy as the nation braces for a widely expected fifth interest rate hike of the year on Tuesday afternoon. In a research paper released on Monday, Commonwealth Bank (CBA) said the Middle East conflict and domestic conditions including high rates and poor productivity are significantly weighing down the economy, and unemployment will rise further than previously expected. The bank’s economists believe growth will fall to just 1 per cent by the middle of next year, almost half of the bank’s previous projection of 1.8 per cent. The gloomy prediction comes as a fifth interest rate rise of the year looks all but certain, putting more pain on households, although it may help the Aussie dollar rise in value. The bank said Australia’s economy was “coming under increasing pressure on several fronts”, with more profound problems remaining even as the Reserve Bank of Australia tries to halt inflation by raising interest rates. “The structural pressures are still acute: continued weak productivity growth, a global AI-induced capex boom putting pressure on interest rates, and supply shocks are keeping inflation higher for longer,” economists Belinda Allen, Ashwin Clarke, Trent Saunders and Harry Ottley wrote on Monday. They noted household spending still remained high despite inflationary pressures – feeding further inflation – and also said the labour market was weaker than first thought. “The labour market is also expected to ease by more than previously expected,” they said, noting that business profits had “deteriorated”. “We now see the unemployment rate increasing to 5.1 per cent compared to our previous peak of 4.8 per cent.” The report also outlined that data centre construction and chip shortages are adding to inflation, even though AI building activity is helping keep the economy ticking over. Headline inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in the 12 months to September, more than expected. CBA said economic weakness would also last longer than expected, with growth not expected to improve to 2.0 per cent until the second half of the 2028 financial year. If there is a silver lining from the predicted rate rise, it’s that the value of the Aussie dollar could rise. “We remain directionally bullish on the AUD,” Barclays said on Monday. “In fact, the RBA could continue to hike even beyond November if the data so requires, notwithstanding market pricing for no more hikes,” it added. As RBA Governor Michele Bullock has outlined in several press conferences this year, a better exchange rate is one of the ways higher interest rates works to lower inflation, as it makes imports cheaper for Australian consumers. However, that may be little relief to many Australians, as CBA warned the rate cuts that are widely expected late next year are no certainty. “Given inflation remains elevated, the rate cuts we have had pencilled in for second half of 2027 remain uncertain,” its economists wrote. “We leave them pencilled in for August and November 2027 but keep only 50 basis points of cuts despite the higher starting point.”

body: Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop. "In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction." He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group. Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance. Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack. The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges. As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street." "We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

US yields are moving higher in the aftermath of both and USD/JPY is at the highs of the day at 158.37. For background, the US Census Bureau’s factory orders report, formally the full report on Manufacturers’ Shipments, Inventories and Orders, is released monthly at 10 am ET, about five weeks after the reference month ends. It arrives roughly a week after the advance durable goods report and expands on it by adding nondurable goods. The headline figure is the monthly change in total new orders for manufactured goods. Nondurables include petroleum and coal products, chemicals, food, paper and plastics. For most nondurable industries, orders are essentially equal to shipments because products aren’t built to order with a backlog. That means swings in oil and commodity prices feed straight into the nondurables figures, since refined petroleum products make up a large share. Markets also look at factory orders excluding transportation, which strips out the volatile aircraft and motor vehicle categories. The report includes revised durable goods data, which sometimes differ meaningfully from the advance estimates. Economists pay close attention to revisions to core capital goods orders and shipments, nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft. Shipments of those goods feed into the equipment investment component of GDP, and the revised figures can shift growth estimates. The release also covers manufacturers’ inventories, unfilled orders and the inventory-to-shipments ratio. These offer a read on whether factories are building or drawing down stock and how much work they have in the pipeline. Because most of the durables data are already known and nondurables largely track commodity prices, factory orders rarely move markets. Its value is in completing the manufacturing picture and providing the revisions that feed into GDP tracking. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: Rystad Energy is an independent energy consulting services and business intelligence provider offering global databases, strategic advisory and research products for energy companies and suppliers,… With the election settled, the presidency continuing for four more years and a newly elected Congress taking office in February, Brazil’s data center policy now hinges on execution, requiring tight coordination between parliament and the executive branch. Most clean tech policies can advance through decrees and agency rules, but data centers are an exception: Unlocking hyperscale investment requires Congress and the executive branch to align statutory tax incentive deadlines with regulatory definitions that are still to be written. At the center is the Redata tax regime (Law No. 15,504/2026), enacted in September to position Brazil as a premier hub for high-performance computing and artificial intelligence. For investors seeking to deploy hyperscale infrastructure, its tax exemptions are neither automatic nor permanent: They are time-bound and contingent on meeting strict operational criteria. Still pending are the executives’ decision on whether natural gas generation qualifies as low-emission power, and critical details on energy-efficiency metrics, local-content requirements and compliance verification. Rystad Energy’s risk assessment reflects this uncertainty, cutting Brazil’s announced data center pipeline by roughly two-thirds, from 21 GW to about 7 GW. Our risk modeling also factors in severe grid congestion and limited access to reliable power, which raise the country’s risk profile for data center development. body: What I Cover My focus spans the global energy landscape and the technologies reshaping it, specifically focusing on oil and gas, renewables, and tech-driven market… The United States and Iran could reach some form of a limited agreement by the middle of 2027, which would allow oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz to continue to gradually recover, but fundamental differences will remain, and the Middle East situation will remain far from normal next year, according to Rystad Energy. “Achieving a comprehensive settlement would require addressing issues related to Iran’s nuclear program, sanctions, Tehran-backed armed groups in the region, and the security of maritime shipping, while also taking into account Israel’s security interests,” Rystad Energy said in a report cited by Azeri news agency Trend . “We consider it unlikely that all these points of contention can be resolved within the coming year,” the analysts led by Rystad’s Head of Geopolitical Analysis, Jorge León, wrote in the report. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz will continue to recover gradually, but are unlikely to reach pre-war levels in a normalized trade flow, according to the energy intelligence firm. Rystad Energy has estimated that crude oil exports from Persian Gulf producers averaged nearly 12 million barrels per day (bpd) in September and the first 20 days of October. “While this is well above the lows recorded earlier in the conflict, it remains substantially below the pre-war level of approximately 18 million barrels per day,” the report reads. While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks, according to Rystad Energy. In the near term, the risk of renewed military escalation following the U.S. midterm elections could be another setback to the recovering Hormuz oil flows. Early on Tuesday, as voting in the midterms began on the U.S. East Coast, oil prices rebounded from Monday’s 7% loss following a Wall Street Journal report about a U.S. strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. At his Budget speech last week, the Chancellor unveiled a new “British Data Centre Covenant” with “strict tests that data centres must meet: To invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies.”? “In return, critical data centres will get the grid connections they need, and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait,” Healey said. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Brent crude plunged more than $6 per barrel Tuesday morning, falling from $107.24 to $100.80 before recovering to around $104 shortly after 10 a.m. Eastern, as traders reacted to a succession of conflicting reports about U.S.-Iran peace negotiations. The selloff followed Monday's 7.6% decline, which left Brent at $104.77. Prices initially rebounded overnight after reports of U.S. strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, before reversing sharply Tuesday morning. The first abrupt decline began moments before a Bloomberg-attributed breaking headline announcing that Iran's supreme leader had authorized negotiations on previously non-negotiable issues. But that was a stronger claim than Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's statement that the supreme leader had only granted the government additional negotiating authority. Pezeshkian had not specified which issues might be discussed. Questions subsequently emerged about whether the Bloomberg headline accurately reflected the Iranian statement. Brent suffered another steep drop around 8:20 a.m, right around the time of an Al Jazeera report that Washington had approved a draft agreement presented through Qatari mediators. Additional reports surfaced that Washington and Tehran had made concessions involving Iran's nuclear program and frozen assets, citing Al Araby Al Jadeed. The Al Araby report described a proposed exchange of Iranian nuclear concessions for the release of frozen funds. But a senior Iranian official has rejected the claim that there was a breakthrough over concessions, and clarified that an agreement was indeed still far off. Tehran’s public position has been and still is that its conditions must be met before Hormuz can reopen, and nuclear negotiations can begin only after those are met. Qatar confirmed that both sides were reviewing proposals, and no agreement has been announced. The competing reports help explain the uncertainty surrounding Tuesday's trading, although they do not establish what caused either sharp decline. Momentum trading and automated orders may have amplified the moves. By midmorning, Brent had recovered nearly $3 from its session low. The reported diplomatic breakthroughs remain unverified, and the Strait of Hormuz remains restricted. body: The curve of the Dubai benchmark is showing signs that rising oil flows from the Middle East are exceeding demand for the first time since early July, when the three-week U.S.-Iran ceasefire allowed millions of barrels to leave unhindered the Strait of Hormuz. Physical flows have been gradually rising for the past two months as Gulf producers accelerated shuttle-shipping through Hormuz with ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, once tankers have cleared the chokepoint. As a result, the November contract of the Dubai benchmark traded at the start of this week at a discount of about $2 per barrel to the December contract, traders and brokers told Bloomberg on Tuesday. This price curve, known as contango, is the first sign since July that current supply is abundant in the Middle East. The contango structure, in which prices for contracts dated further out in time are higher than the prompt contracts, suggests that concerns about the immediate lack of crude supply have eased significantly. Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices in recent weeks, prompting increased buying from Asian refiners, especially those in India who have preferred additional Middle Eastern cargoes to the more expensive Russian barrels with higher freight costs. At the end of last month, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recover and reach pre-war levels in some days and weeks. In contrast with the international benchmark futures prices, the prices of physical crudes from the Middle East have softened, as oil continues to flow out of the Persian Gulf at volumes close to pre-war levels, excluding Iran. Two weeks ago, robust crude oil flows out of the Middle East started to pressure the key metric of strength for physical supply out of the region. The premium of Oman crude over Dubai, the measure of the Middle East’s market strength, slumped to the lowest level since the end of July. BPCL has bought the cargo for delivery at Mumbai in late December-early January, paying a premium of some $18 per barrel over Dated Brent, according to Reuters' sources. Last week, BPCL said it would reduce its purchases of crude oil from Russia in November as high freight costs and premiums for Russia's crude undermine the attractiveness of Moscow's oil compared to Middle Eastern offers. The refiner will buy lower volumes of Russian crude in November as the Middle East grades are more commercially attractive for the company now, BPCL's head of finance, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, said. Russian crude oil accounted for 37% of BPCL's crude supplies in the quarter July to September, the executive said. But the purchases of Russian cargoes for November will be "significantly reduced" due to the higher shipping costs, according to Gupta. BPCL's crude sourcing decision is generally in line with the recent trend for lower imports of Russian crude oil in India, due to the higher costs compared to Middle Eastern cargoes, whose availability has increased with the rise of flows through the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, eased freight rates in the past two weeks have prompted Asian crude oil buyers, Chinese in particular, to seek cargoes from Brazil and West Africa. Freight rates have eased from the record highs seen in early October, but they were still about $60 million for a supertanker to carry oil from the U.S. to Asia in the middle of October. The cost was so high that Asian refiners weren't ordering much crude from the U.S. for November delivery. title: Canada gold output jumps 22% as global supply slips
summary: Growth shows how new operations are adding meaningful volumes while some established mining countries struggle with lower grades and changing mine plans.
body: Canadian gold production jumped 22% in the third quarter as new mines increased output, outpacing global growth even as rising costs made ounces more expensive to produce. Recently commissioned operations including Equinox Gold’s (TSX, NYSE-A: EQX) Valentine mine in Newfoundland and Labrador and B2Gold’s (TSX: BTO; NYSE-A: BTG) Goose mine in Nunavut helped drive the increase, alongside stronger production from existing mines, the World Gold Council said Tuesday. Worldwide mine output rose 3% to a third-quarter record of 1,071 tonnes. “Mine production could reach another record high, but the overall supply response should remain modest, with recycling still subdued,” the Council said in its latest quarterly assessment . Canada’s growth shows how new operations are adding meaningful volumes while some established mining countries struggle with lower grades and changing mine plans. Yet increased mine production has not translated into more total supply: weaker recycling and a further reduction in producers’ outstanding hedges pushed the global total 1% lower to 1,369 tonnes. Valentine entered commercial production in November last year, giving this year’s third quarter a much larger contribution than the commissioning period a year earlier. The Newfoundland operation is expected to produce 140,000 to 150,000 oz. this year, according to Equinox’s operating outlook . Canada was among several countries recording substantial gains. Indonesian output increased 21%, helped by higher grades and production at Batu Hijau, the start of Pani Gold and recovering output at Grasberg. Chilean production rose 19%, supported by Salares Norte and the newly commissioned Fenix operation, the council said. Those increases contrasted with a 12% decline in Australia and a 7% fall in the United States. Lower-grade mining and production sequencing weighed on both countries, including at Cadia in Australia and Nevada Gold Mines and Round Mountain in the U.S. Global mine production was 2% higher over the first nine months, putting the industry on course for a full-year record unless widespread disappointments emerge in the fourth quarter, the Council said. The additional output comes at a higher cost. Average industry all-in sustaining costs reached a record C$2,698 ($1,930) per oz. in the second quarter, up 22% from a year earlier, according to Metals Focus data cited by the Council. The figures, which lag production data by a quarter, showed the fastest annual cost increase since early 2013. Higher energy and consumable prices, along with increased sustaining capital spending, contributed to the rise. BMO Capital Markets’ latest GoldPages estimates point in the same direction. Production-weighted sustaining costs for producers covered by the bank are forecast to average $1,795 per oz. this year, 16% more than in 2025. Including development capital, average all-in costs are forecast to rise 22% to $2,298 per ounce. The BMO figures cover a different group of companies and a full year, so they are not directly comparable with the council’s quarterly industry estimate. The bank forecasts some relief next year, with sustaining costs easing to $1,764 per ounce. Gold prices remain well above those cost measures. Bullion averaged $4,262 per oz. in the third quarter, 23% more than a year earlier, according to the council. However, sustaining costs exclude development spending and do not measure a company’s full cash requirements. Recycled supply fell 8% to about 314 tonnes in the third quarter, its lowest level since late 2023. The decline outweighed the increase in mined gold, alongside an estimated 17-tonne reduction in outstanding producer hedges. Recycling remained subdued despite historically high prices. In India, some owners preferred to pledge gold as collateral, while jewellery exchanges allowed buyers to fund new purchases with old pieces. title: JPMorgan sees US copper output more than doubling
summary: New mine developments and expansions could transform American supply, but high costs and permitting remain major hurdles.
body: JPMorgan (NYSE) sees potential for the US to more than double its annual mined copper production through new projects and expansions, reversing decades of decline as Washington pushes to secure domestic critical minerals supplies. The investment bank estimates the country could add 1.3 million tonnes of annual copper capacity, ranking it third globally for potential supply growth behind Chile and Argentina. However, most of that production is unlikely to come online until after 2030. US copper output has halved over the past 30 years to roughly 1 million tonnes annually, largely because of underinvestment, JPMorgan estimates. The country’s share of global production has plunged from about 50% in 1900 to less than 5% today. The potential revival comes as the US seeks to reduce its dependence on foreign mineral supplies. But higher development costs, lengthy permitting processes and limited domestic processing capacity could constrain how quickly new mines contribute to production. The proposed Resolution Copper mine in Arizona accounts for roughly half of the additional US copper capacity identified by JPMorgan, making it central to the bank’s long-term growth outlook. The underground project, a joint venture between Rio Tinto (ASX: RIO) and BHP (ASX: BHP), could produce about 18 million tonnes of copper over a 40-year mine life, according to the companies. At full production, it could meet as much as 25% of US copper demand. However, Resolution still faces permitting requirements and technical studies, with production unlikely to begin before 2030. Development costs present another obstacle. JPMorgan estimates US copper projects require about $28,000 in capital investment for each tonne of annual production capacity, compared with a global average of $26,000. The higher costs could weigh on project economics, particularly for large underground developments requiring substantial infrastructure before production begins. JPMorgan identifies Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE), the largest US copper producer, as one of the best-positioned companies to expand domestic output in the medium term. The bank estimates Freeport has more than 250,000 tonnes of potential annual production growth from brownfield expansions at existing operations. Such projects could deliver copper sooner than new mines because they can use established infrastructure and avoid some of the permitting and construction challenges facing greenfield developments. Regulatory changes could also improve the outlook. The US FAST-41 framework, established in 2025 to streamline federal reviews of major infrastructure projects, offers a potential route to shorter permitting timelines for eligible mines. Advances in in-situ leaching , which extracts copper from ore without conventional excavation, and the restart of idled mines could provide further production gains, JPMorgan says. Yet expanding mine output alone would not guarantee greater US copper self-sufficiency. The country faces a primary copper supply deficit of about 1 million tonnes and would need additional smelting and refining capacity to process more domestically mined concentrate. That leaves the pace of investment in processing infrastructure, alongside mine development, as a key factor in determining how much of the potential production increase translates into a stronger domestic copper supply chain. If equity-market losses trigger liquidity needs, investors are more likely to sell gold than buy.

title: Sunshine Silver weighs doubling mill capacity
summary: The proposed plant would process up to 2,000 tonnes a day compared with about 1,000 tonnes in the initial assessment.
body: Sunshine Silver Mining & Refining (NYSE: SSMR) is designing a mill with roughly twice the capacity assumed in its initial mine plan, seeking room to expand production after a targeted late-2028 restart in Idaho. The proposed plant would process up to 2,000 tonnes a day compared with about 1,000 tonnes in the initial assessment, according to the company’s second-quarter filing. The Sunshine silver mine lies near Kellogg in Idaho’s Silver Valley, about 430 km north of the state capital, Boise. “Clearly, getting those feasibility studies wrapped up first half of next year, that will position us to look at what remaining capital would be needed to fund us all the way through to production,” CFO Heather White told The Northern Miner in late September at the Mining Forum Americas in Colorado. The larger mill is to give Sunshine room to increase output as drilling expands and upgrades its resource. But the company’s March initial assessment estimated capital costs for a smaller operation. Next year’s feasibility study must establish whether the mine can support higher throughput and how much additional funding the restart requires. A new mine entrance should give Sunshine more flexibility in the Upper Country area, where drilling suggests potential resource growth and a larger contribution to the mine plan, BMO Capital Markets analyst Kevin O’Halloran wrote in an Oct. 19 note. Sunshine expects to complete the mine-and-mill feasibility study in the second quarter of next year before making a final investment decision. The initial assessment estimated capital spending at $286.9 million (C$409.2 million) for the smaller operation, according to company disclosures. That plan forecast average annual silver production of 6.7 million oz. over the first five years of a 24-year mine life. Those projections don’t describe the proposed larger operation. Sunshine raised $310.5 million before expenses in its June initial public offering, including the underwriters’ full exercise of their option to purchase additional shares. Net proceeds totalled $286.5 million, according to an investor presentation in September. Crews are dismantling the old mill, and the company has installed a new hoist and purchased underground equipment. A working shaft and a tunnel into the mine’s upper levels provide access to the deposit, White said. Replacing the existing infrastructure would cost about $600 million, the company estimates. A 50,000-metre underground drilling program aims chiefly to upgrade inferred resources to the higher-confidence indicated category for the feasibility study. Sunshine expects to finish the program this month and report results from deeper parts of the mine this quarter, it said in its September exploration update. The February resource estimate outlined 3.16 million indicated tonnes grading 1,022 grams silver per tonne for 103.9 million ounces. Inferred resources totalled 6.41 million tonnes grading 776 grams for 159.8 million ounces. The initial assessment’s production plan includes both categories. body: The Democratic Republic of Congo has ordered an investigation into suspected illegal mining after authorities seized thousands of tons of copper and cobalt in a widening crackdown across the country’s mineral-rich southeast. A commission comprising police, military and mines ministry officials confiscated more than 500 trucks and other vehicles and machinery during operations in Lualaba and Haut-Katanga provinces, the justice ministry said in a statement posted Monday on X . Justice Minister Guillaume Ngefa Atondoko Andali ordered the investigation after the commission uncovered suspected mining fraud, unauthorized exploitation of mineral resources and mineral smuggling. The action highlights Congo’s struggle to control illegal mining on concessions held by major international companies. The country is the world’s largest cobalt producer and second-biggest copper producer, making enforcement critical to protecting operations that supply global metals markets. The seizures took place at several sites, including Menda in Lualaba province, where Eurasian Resources Group (ERG) holds mining licences. ERG has complained in recent months about illegal mining on its concessions, including at its flagship Metalkol copper-cobalt operation. The investigation follows a series of enforcement measures targeting unauthorized mining activity in the country’s copper belt. Last week, Mines Minister Louis Kabamba Watum suspended the head of state artisanal mining agency SAEMAPE , accusing him of failing to prevent illegal operations on licensed concessions. Authorities have also detained more than 300 foreign nationals , mainly Chinese citizens, in operations concentrated around Kolwezi, a major mining hub in Lualaba province. Congolese civilians and military personnel were also reportedly arrested. The crackdown on Chinese nationals suspected of illegal mining comes despite the prominent presence of Chinese mining companies, including CMOC (HKG:03993) and Zijin Mining (HKG:2899), which account for a substantial share of Congo’s copper and cobalt production. At just over US$3,900 this morning, an ounce of gold has sunk back to where it was trading last autumn, down more than 8 per cent this year and about 25 per cent from its peak last February. A number of forces have been working against the yellow metal. Higher real yields and lately a stronger U.S. dollar have made gold — which doesn’t pay any interest — less desirable. The artificial intelligence boom has attracted investor dollars to riskier assets. The consensus view is that gold will eventually pull out of the spiral and average US$4,600 in the last quarter of 2027, but that’s not how Capital Economics sees it. While central bank buying will limit some of the downside, Capital expects gold to come under even more pressure in 2027. Capital economists expect a total of three rate hikes from the Fed, but acknowledge the odds lean to more. While gold often rebounds later in equity bear markets that’s usually because the Fed cuts interest rates during these periods. Capital expects no such intervention this time. Gold has also lost its edge as an effective hedge during market turmoil because of its close correlation to equities over the past few years, said Tompkins.
